La communauté s’unit grâce à la Kwanzaa: The community comes together through Kwanzaa
Pour plusieurs afro-descendants d’Amériq: For many people of African descent in North America, December 26 marks the start of Kwanzaa, which runs until January 1.
Cela semble être un temps des Fêtes part: This seems to be a particularly difficult holiday season for many, much like the year that came before it. Many of us, like me, have had to rethink our traditions in a different context. In that spirit, I want to bring a bit of light to this darkened time, along with some ideas for celebrating in a way that feels closer to our convictions.
Le lendemain de Noël, on allume la premi: The day after Christmas, the first of the seven candles of the kinara, the seven-branched candleholder made for the occasion, is lit. The first candle, umoja, celebrates unity. It is black and sits in the middle of the kinara.
L’unité, c’est le moteur de Seti Dibanda: Unity is what drives Seti Dibanda, president of Afrocentricité Internationale Montréal (AI). “Our organization brings together Africans and people of African descent in Canada and around the world. We are active in many countries, in the Americas, in Europe, and even on the African continent,” says the man who has led AI’s Montréal chapter for nearly 10 years.
On rejoint M. Dibanda à son domicile de: We reach Mr. Dibanda at his home in Montréal, as holiday preparations are in full swing. On this December afternoon, he takes the time to talk with us while looking after his one-year-old son, the rest of the family having gone out to run errands.
Depuis 2015, AI Montréal est l’hôte d’un: Since 2015, AI Montréal has hosted a large public Kwanzaa celebration. “We organize a gala evening where we try to bring the community together, Africans and people of African descent from all over the world. We really try to gather people and celebrate the culture,” says Mr. Dibanda.
Au cours de cette soirée, on explique d’: During the evening, the history of the holiday and its purpose are explained first. The word “Kwanzaa,” taken from the Swahili phrase “matunda ya kwanza,” means “first fruits.” It is a seven-day celebration inspired by traditional African harvest festivals. Because the word “Kwanza” has only six letters, an extra “a” was added so that its seven letters would correspond to the seven principles of Kwanzaa, or “nguzo saba” in Swahili. Its founder, Maulana Karenga, wanted to “give Black people an alternative to Christmas and an opportunity to celebrate themselves and their history, rather than simply imitating the practices of the dominant society.”
« Je parle de la table qui est construit: “I talk about the table that is set up, and about the nguzo saba, the seven principles of Kwanzaa, and about the impact on the community, about how to lift ourselves up. We also give thanks to the ancestors,” adds Mr. Dibanda.
À l’occasion de la fête, on déploie un t: For the holiday, a straw mat is laid out to represent the community, and fruits and vegetables are placed on top of it, referring to the collective harvests of African villagers. Among them is corn, which symbolizes the children of each family, along with a cup, which stands for sharing. Handmade gifts and offerings are also included, evoking creativity and intention. The kinara, the seven-branched candleholder, also sits on the mat. The candles, three red, three green and one black, represent the Pan-African flag, which symbolizes the unity of African peoples.
Seti Dibanda explique que la Kwanzaa est: Seti Dibanda explains that Kwanzaa is an Afrocentric holiday, Afrocentricity being an ideology that seeks to put Africans back at the centre of their own existence. The celebration originated in the United States, where it was established in 1966 by Professor Maulana Karenga, who headed the Africana studies department at California State University. He wanted to support African American culture and unite Black communities in the wake of the violent racial riots that took place in Los Angeles in 1965.
« C’était la période des émancipations e: “It was the era of emancipation and civil rights. You have to emancipate yourself, but there is an identity you have to preserve,” says Mr. Dibanda. “The founder’s concern was to create ties between Africans on the continent and African Americans. That’s why he based Kwanzaa on the harvest festival, which already existed on the continent. It’s a holiday that puts Afrocentric culture and values forward. As an organization, we embrace it and celebrate it,” he adds.
À Afrocentricité Internationale Montréal: At Afrocentricité Internationale Montréal, the celebration has taken on all kinds of colours over the years. Sometimes there has been poetry performed by children, while on other occasions a musical performance has been the highlight, whether a percussion group or a choreographed dance troupe. This year, there will be an African fashion show, during which prizes will be awarded to participants. As every year, a buffet of African and Caribbean specialties will be served and, of course, the dance floor will be open to anyone who wants to get moving – a must, he hints.
En allumant les bougies de la Kwanzaa, l: When lighting the Kwanzaa candles, the flame must spread from the centre of the kinara outward. The black candle, lit on December 26, sits at the centre. Then there are three green candles on the left and three red candles on the right, all evoking the Pan-African flag. On December 27, the second day of Kwanzaa, the kujichagulia candle is lit to celebrate self-determination. The third day is ujima, which represents collective work. On the fourth, ujamaa, or cooperative economics, is celebrated. On the fifth, a candle is lit for nia, the principle of purpose and community building. On the sixth day, kuumba, creativity, is honoured. Finally, the last candle represents imani, that is, faith.
Pour Seti Dibanda, la Kwanzaa débute à l: For Seti Dibanda, Kwanzaa begins at home with his wife and three children. For the father of the family, it is a special time. For the occasion, a table is set and decorated with artwork, fruits and vegetables. “What matters is that everyone drinks from the cup of unity. It’s an act that creates communion with the family,” he says.
La Kwanzaa est une célébration publique,: Kwanzaa is a public celebration in which everyone can take part. The holiday has been officially celebrated in Canada since 1993. “Canada is a country where communities are recognized and have the opportunity to express themselves. Here in Canada, it’s possible to keep your identity while embracing Canadian values,” says Mr. Dibanda of his adopted country. Born in Cameroon, he chose Canada after pursuing studies in Germany.
« Mon nom de famille est Quansah », dit: “My last name is Quansah,” says Randy Quansah with a laugh, pronouncing his name like the name of the Kwanzaa holiday. Born in Montréal, he is about to celebrate Kwanzaa with his eight-year-old daughter in Calgary, where he has lived for 14 years.
S’il a entendu parler pour la première f: Although he first heard about the holiday as a teenager, it was when he became a father that he truly started looking into how to celebrate it. “The idea of culture and history really resonated with me after my child was born. I asked myself how I wanted her to deal with the experience of being Black,” he says. That reflection led him to revisit Black histories and do his own research. “You feel more responsible for telling the story, or at least for sparking [your child’s] curiosity so that they want to know more,” he says.
Son expérience auprès des enfants lui mo: His experience with children showed him the way forward. “I told myself that change had to start with children, because they’re open-minded. And children have the ability to hold their parents and guardians accountable. They’ll say to you, ‘Hey, you said that, remember what you said,’” notes the teacher.
L’un des épisodes de la série Kujo’s Kid: One of the episodes of the series Kujo’s Kid Zone, which he hosts on YouTube, features Jeanette Epps, a NASA astronaut. She is the first Black woman to have travelled to a space station. “I realized we have the opportunity to bring about all kinds of social change through the. Am I the person who’s going to change everything? Probably not, but at some point, someone, a child, will see this and be inspired by it. That’s the beauty of it!” says Mr. Quansah.
Ce dernier fait alors le lien avec la Kw: He then makes the connection to Kwanzaa, which was the subject of one of the series’ episodes. He believes that Black people – of all languages and all cultures – need to understand their culture and heritage. “That’s the whole importance of this celebration – it allows the community to better understand that heritage,” he says.
Selon Randy Quansah, « l’état d’esprit d: According to Randy Quansah, an “abundance mindset” is what originally set African peoples apart from European colonizers. By this expression, he means the conviction that one has all the resources needed to provide for everyone. “Capitalism is a scarcity mindset, the idea that there aren’t enough resources for everyone. Europeans had a spirit of conquest because in their respective countries, there weren’t enough resources,” says Mr. Quansah.
Il dresse le parallèle avec les peuples: He draws a parallel with Indigenous peoples. “Indigenous peoples of North America have always had this abundance mindset, for example thinking: ‘How can I say this land belongs to someone? How can I say it belongs to me?’” The same goes for the African continent, which, in his view, controls and runs the world by holding resources that are vital today. “If there’s no Africa, there’s no world. All your resources, your cell phones, your gold, your diamonds, your food, your chocolate come from the African continent,” says Mr. Quansah.
Il ajoute que c’est cette abondance en m: He adds that it is this abundance of raw materials that, paradoxically, has left the people of the African continent the worst off on earth. “Historically, the African continent has been the greatest threat to the rest of the world. It has the largest number of people and the most resources. But Africans have no intention of going around the world and conquering it. They don’t feel the need to,” he says. Added to that mindset is one of collective use of resources, that is, the habit of not taking credit for the many innovations – agricultural, technological, cultural and more – that we owe to African and Afro-descendant communities.
M. Quansah souligne l’importance, pour l: Mr. Quansah stresses how important it is for Africans in the diaspora to remember who they are, beyond the stigmatization and the losses – slavery, colonization, human exploitation, racism. “That’s the whole point of the creation of Kwanzaa: we need to remember who we are. We need to have a goal to reach, to have collective responsibilities within our group, to have faith in ourselves. We need to go back and reassess our goals, rediscover our creativity,” says the teacher. “These are principles of community and an encouragement toward a greater community.”
Peu importe la culture ou la religion de: Regardless of the culture or religion of those who celebrate it, Kwanzaa fits into everyone’s life. “These principles are so universal and incredible that you can apply them even if you’re not Black.” Randy Quansah hopes this celebration will be as widely recognized as Christmas or Hanukkah. “But we often get the feeling that when you bring up something specific to Black culture, there’s always hesitation. Like Black History Month, for example,” he observes.
Il souhaite donc qu’avec la Kwanzaa, la: He therefore hopes that through Kwanzaa, the diaspora and people of African descent can be proud of themselves. “Self-pride is something very, very important. I love that people are starting to wear their hair natural, to wear more traditional clothing and things like that, because all of these things contribute to a sense of pride. And when you feel a sense of pride, what comes next is the desire to have a purpose.”
Chez M. Quansah, les chandelles sont prê: At Mr. Quansah’s home, the candles are ready to be lit. The straw mat will be placed on a table, with fruits and vegetables on top. “During Kwanzaa, you focus on one element each day. That’s what I’m going to do and celebrate with my daughter, so that she too gets into that mindset. I hope it becomes an annual tradition that we can build together, she and I, and that when she has her own family, she can make it part of her own activities.”
